questions.explain: The chapter identifies three waste categories in non-production: always-on instances idle outside business hours (fix: stop/start schedules), oversized instances mirroring production specs (fix: right-size to workload), and unnecessary Multi-AZ (fix: convert to Single-AZ).
options: Always-on outside business hours, oversized to mirror production, and unnecessary Multi-AZ
Too many regions, too many backups, too many tags
Over-provisioned storage, unused read replicas, excessive log retention
License costs, support plans, and data transfer fees
questions.q: What are the three waste categories behind most non-production database overspend?

questions.explain: The chapter distinguishes functional correctness testing (instance one to two tiers smaller than production is almost always adequate) from performance testing (a dedicated perf environment on production-sized hardware for a few hours per week is far cheaper than full-size instances 24/7). Also: convert Multi-AZ dev/QA to Single-AZ to halve compute cost.
options: Mirror production exactly in every environment to be safe
Use production-sized instances but turn them off monthly
For correctness testing use 1–2 tiers smaller than production; for performance testing use a dedicated prod-sized environment for a few hours per week; convert non-prod Multi-AZ to Single-AZ
Non-production should always use the cheapest possible tier regardless of workload
questions.q: What is the chapter's right-sizing guidance for non-production instances?

questions.explain: A dev database running weekdays 7 AM–7 PM runs 60 of 168 hours — a 64% compute-hour reduction. AWS has a hard limit: RDS instances auto-restart after 7 days if left stopped, so schedules must handle that, and a self-service developer override (e.g., SSM Automation document) keeps late/weekend work unblocked.
options: About 10–15%; stop/start is rarely worth the effort
Roughly 64% of compute hours eliminated for a weekday business-hours pattern; AWS auto-restarts stopped RDS instances after 7 days, so schedules must account for that
100% — storage is also free while stopped
Scheduling saves nothing on SQL Server because of license-included pricing
questions.q: How much can stop/start schedules save, and what AWS limit must automation handle?

questions.explain: Teams size dev instances for connection count rather than data: without pooling, hundreds of mostly-idle sessions consume worker threads and memory. RDS Proxy does not support SQL Server at all — the fix is client-side pooling (ADO.NET/ODBC/JDBC pool by default) with disciplined Max Pool Size (e.g., 25) and Min Pool Size=0; if sleeping sessions exceed ~40–70%, tightening pools lets you drop 1–2 tiers.
options: Buy RDS Proxy for SQL Server
Disable connection pooling entirely
Increase Max Pool Size to 1000
Use client-side pooling with a disciplined Max Pool Size (RDS Proxy doesn't support SQL Server); if sleeping sessions exceed ~40–70% of total, tighten pools and drop 1–2 instance tiers
questions.q: How does connection overhead drive false instance sizing, and what is the fix on RDS for SQL Server?

questions.explain: Governance: apply SCPs to the non-production OU denying oversized instance classes and Multi-AZ=true; use Azure Policy to deny >4 vCore non-prod databases; enforce guardrails in shared Terraform modules; and run weekly automated cost reports to Slack so non-prod spending is visible with clear ownership.
options: SCPs denying oversized classes and Multi-AZ in non-prod, Azure Policy vCore limits, Terraform module validation, and weekly automated cost reports to Slack
Rely on manual code review of every Terraform change
Only allow the DBA team to provision anything
Governance is unnecessary once schedules are in place
questions.q: What governance controls prevent non-production environments from drifting back to oversized configurations?

title: Dev and Test Cost Reduction: Schedules and Smaller Instances
